title: TURKESTERONE / ECDYSTERONE MARKETING SCHEMES: How Supplements Companies TRICK you
summary: A long analysis of how the supplement industry sells products people don't need, from magazine-era whey protein hype to the influencer and paid meme campaigns behind turkesterone and ecdysterone. He argues these products are mostly marketing, debunks the 'it's in spinach/quinoa' defence, and urges viewers to cut doses, go without supplements and judge sellers by their financial ties.
claims: Once you understand how supplement marketing works you can recognise it and become immune to it; he openly opposes the supplement industry
The supplement industry is a conglomerate of competing companies whose shared goal is to empty your wallet by any means necessary, and it has infiltrated every fitness sphere through sponsorships
The supplement industry sells about $35 billion a year with roughly 3% annual growth, has never shrunk, and is valued around $140 billion in total
Unlike dairy or textiles, the supplement industry is barely 100 years old, which makes its growth a remarkable success story
The supplement industry and pro (enhanced) bodybuilding grew together in a symbiotic relationship: pros need sponsor money, companies need pros to push products
Pro bodybuilding overtook natural bodybuilding partly because supplement companies backed it; naturals focused on their own body and good food and were useless as salesmen
Supplement money fuelled pro bodybuilders' drug habits and helped shift the culture away from natural bodybuilding, which he calls the perfect crime
In the 70s and 80s magazines like Joe Weider's Muscle & Fitness sold his own supplements next to photos of drugged pros, implying the product built the physique
Weider sold his nutrition company to a food company for a huge sum; food companies care about selling, not health or effectiveness, which turned supplements into a cash machine
Whey protein was the first big hype supplement, sold as a magic potion that builds muscle without effort; in reality it only makes protein easier to consume
Most lifters take far too much protein powder and treat it as a ritual; he was one of them
The anabolic window was a marketing tactic to make people drink more protein powder
About 0.8 g of protein per pound of bodyweight is close to optimal
Studies test what is optimal but never test lower intakes, so 'suboptimal' protein may still give 94-95% of the gains; less protein than recommended can still give nearly the same gains
Old-school bodybuilders ate less protein than today's lifters, only from real food like steak and eggs, and still built great physiques
He has never taken turkesterone or ecdysterone and never intends to; the video is about marketing rather than a product review
Marketing strategy 1 is to create a need: make you believe the product is a missing building block and that you lose out without it
Strategy 2 is suggestion: ads hint that you might not get enough protein, planting a doubt instead of saying it outright; with no competing idea, the suggested idea wins
Strategy 3 is fear of missing out, which exploits our evolved fear of scarcity; companies hire psychologists to tap into it
Bulk discounts exist because the more product you have at home, the faster you consume it; buy three tubs and you'll drink more protein
Protein powder isn't physically addictive but stockpiling creates psychological dependence; stimulants are physically addictive through caffeine so they need less marketing
Modern marketing turns wants into needs, and once accepted those needs stay for life, tying consumers emotionally to the product
The way out is experience: stop or reduce protein powder for a while and watch your progress; nine times out of ten nothing changes
He went from protein powder three times a day to about two scoops a week with no loss of weight or gains, and feels he wasted hundreds or thousands of dollars
Take half the recommended dose of any supplement (half a scoop of protein or pre-workout); results are the same and you buy half as many tubs
Creatine loading phases are useless and exist only to make you use up the product faster
Packaging is a distraction; supplement companies make their money by shaping culture, with community memes and jokes making protein powder seem indispensable
Viral marketing comes in two types: piggyback (riding an existing meme) and sponsor (starting the meme); turkesterone and ecdysterone were sold with the sponsor type
Memes are ideal Trojan horses: repeatable, funny, aimed at the young, unlabelled, untraceable and exempt from the disclosure rules that apply to TV ads
TV and billboard ads barely affect sales because viewers are on guard; ads work best when you don't know you are watching one
By his research, 96-98.2% of exposure to turkesterone and ecdysterone came from viral campaigns on YouTube, Instagram and TikTok
Laughing at the guy selling 'big balls' rat-study pills or toxic-poop cleanses is pointless: tens of thousands bought them, and turkesterone buyers fell for subtler versions of the same thing
Influencer playbook: act clueless in a neutral first video, then about 3-4 months later launch your own product; real production takes longer, so the product was already in the works
Fake out-of-stock announcements build scarcity and urgency, so people buy three tubs instead of one at relaunch, often with a sale on top
The fear of leaving gains on the table makes lifters chase optimal protein and stack products they don't need
Sellers twist turkesterone and ecdysterone studies, knowing buyers won't check the sources; he works with data and says numbers can be made to say anything
Food, pharma and supplement industries fund studies to label products 'scientific'; science used to push products stops being science and becomes marketing
A YouTuber 'tested' turkesterone after dieting in a deficit and losing muscle for a month, then credited the supplement for regains that were really muscle memory
Ignore anyone who earns money or a cut from a supplement; money corrupts both people and the truth
Comparing ecdysterone to spinach is a straw man: eat spinach freely, but don't buy an extract that costs about 300 times more and gives less benefit
Ecdysterone sells for about $60 a small bottle at a margin near 200%; product prices are unrelated to manufacturing cost, like Nike shoes
Creatine is one of the most proven and potent supplements, yet one tub of ecdysterone costs as much as six tubs of creatine; the price gap is marketing, not potency
Marketing potency scale: TV ad 1, YouTube ad 2, influencer promotion 3, grassroots paid campaigns 4; the less you know it's an ad, the harder it is to resist
Companies pay workers to post memes from fake accounts; he cites Bird Box, AirPods and Squid Game as paid campaigns and the Fast and Furious family meme as a flop
He left negative reviews on 12-15 turkesterone/ecdysterone sites and 95% were deleted
Fake comment accounts push turkesterone: untraceable names, muscular stock profile pictures, histories that only defend the product, and copy-pasted claims like '20 lb on my bench'
Any gains on turkesterone come from placebo or from training harder because you believe in it; keep training the same without it and gains are equal
Vegans eat lots of ecdysterone-rich quinoa yet aren't known for size, which undermines the hype
Megadoses don't scale gains: creatine powder is about 20 times denser than red meat but doesn't give 20 times the gains; the body has a threshold
Show me the monsters: these products have been around for years, yet nobody bigger than top naturals got there on them
Every magic pill is either a laced steroid that alters hormones or a dud; the few that work, like creatine, don't justify $60
He has watched a new magic pill appear every six months or year in about 12 years of YouTube fitness, and old ones get recycled years later
Most people selling these pills are on steroids, so their gains come from drugs, not the supplement
The same YouTubers sold SARMs when they were legally grey and now push TRT to teenagers; honest SARM users showed little physique change over two years
He predicts the next magic supplement will be a black pepper or capsaicin extract, based on studies linking spicy food to higher testosterone
